newsitem.title: KUWAIT: Kuwait explains need for U.S. help to contain Iraq.
newsitem.headline: Kuwait explains need for U.S. help to contain Iraq.

text.p: Kuwaiti ministers toured Arab capitals on Tuesday to stress the need for U.S. military help to deter "threats" by its former occupier Iraq.

The ministers of defence and information are touring fellow members of the 1991 Gulf War Damascus Declaration Arab alliance to rally support for Kuwait's decision to allow U.S. troops and Stealth bombers to deploy in the tiny Gulf Arab state.
The six oil-rich Gulf Cooperation Council (GCC) states had originally sealed the pact with Egypt and Syria for their military presence in the region in return for economic help.
But the collective military component was later scrapped as some GCC states favoured Western, mainly U.S., help -- a move which angered the two allies and threatened to ruin the pact.
Saudi Arabia, the United Arab Emirates, Oman, Kuwait, Qatar and Bahrain make up the GCC.

After a brief misunderstanding and contradicting signals by Washington, President Bill Clinton said on Tuesday he had signed an order to deploy U.S. ground troops in Kuwait but did not say when they might actually leave.

Minutes later Kuwait television carried the news, saying that 3,500 soldiers would be involved in the deployment which is part of a major U.S. build-up in the region for a possible strike against Iraq.

The touring Kuwaiti ministers are telling their hosts that Iraq last week called the deployment of the Stealth an act of war. Kuwait says it is a new threat that has not been retracted by a country that occupied it for seven months.

"We don't deal with words but with realities which we see clearly in Iraq's south and these are worrying," Information Minister Sheikh Saud Nasser al-Saud al-Sabah said after talks in Egypt with President Hosni Mubarak. He later flew to Syria.

While Egypt and Syria continue to support Kuwait's right to defend itself if attacked by Iraq, they have not endorsed the latest U.S. flap with Iraq and oppose the September 3 and 4 cruise missile attacks against targets in southern Iraq.

Cairo and Damascus, like most of the Arab world, saw as legitimate Baghdad's military intervention in northern Iraq which did not violate United Nations Gulf crisis-related resolutions or international norms.

In the Gulf, Kuwait's Defence Minister Sheikh Ahmad Hamoud al-Jaber al-Sabah held talks with Saudi King Fahd on the first leg of a tour of GCC states, which with varrying degrees are concerned over the outcome of wider strikes against Iraq.
Two added Patriot missile batteries and their U.S. crews arrived in Saudi Arabia in response to the latest tension. A third Scud-busting Patriot battery was also ordered for Kuwait.

Despite the apparent lack of support for Washington, Western analysts in Kuwait said a fresh attack on Iraq would not destroy the 1991 coalition if targets were limited to air defences in the no-fly zones in northern and southern Iraq.
One said Washington's standoff with Iraq was now at "a lull or a pause" but the issue was still "unresolved...unsettled".
A senior Gulf Arab military official said Gulf states that oppose hitting targets inside the no-fly zone "would reluctantly stay silent" if U.S. attacks were limited.
But, said the non-Kuwaiti officer: "A wider attack will ruin everthing and could split the coalition."
